subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: E. coli food poisoning is often linked to:
options: Undercooked minced beef and contaminated water
questions.explain: E. coli is commonly associated with undercooked minced beef, raw milk and contaminated water.

questions.q: To prevent cross-contamination, raw meat should be stored in the fridge:
options: On the top shelf above other foods
On the bottom shelf below ready-to-eat foods
questions.explain: Raw meat is stored on the bottom shelf so its juices cannot drip onto ready-to-eat foods.

questions.q: Which practice helps prevent bacteria multiplying when cooling cooked food before refrigerating?
options: Putting hot food straight into a sealed warm cupboard
Cooling it quickly within about 1-2 hours then refrigerating
questions.explain: Cooked food should be cooled quickly (within 1-2 hours) and refrigerated to limit time in the danger zone.

questions.q: A 'use-by' date on a food product tells you:
options: When the food should be frozen
The last date the food is safe to eat
The date by which the food is at its best quality only
questions.explain: A use-by date is a safety date; eating the food after it is unsafe even if it looks fine.

questions.q: A 'best-before' date mainly refers to a food's:
options: Quality, such as flavour and texture
questions.explain: A best-before date relates to quality; food may still be safe to eat after this date but may be lower quality.

questions.q: Campylobacter, a common cause of food poisoning, is most often associated with:
questions.explain: Campylobacter is most commonly found on raw and undercooked chicken and other poultry.

questions.q: Listeria is of particular concern for pregnant women and is associated with which foods?
questions.explain: Listeria can grow in chilled foods such as unpasteurised soft cheeses and pate, posing a risk in pregnancy.

questions.q: The recommended temperature for a freezer is:
questions.explain: A freezer should be kept at -18C or below, which makes bacteria dormant.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of cross-contamination?
options: Using the same chopping board for raw chicken and salad without washing it
questions.explain: Cross-contamination is the transfer of bacteria from raw food to ready-to-eat food, such as via an unwashed board.

questions.q: Which type of food is classed as 'high-risk' for food poisoning?
questions.explain: High-risk foods are moist, protein-rich, ready-to-eat foods such as cooked meat and cooked rice.

questions.q: Some bacteria are hard to destroy by normal cooking because they can:
options: Form heat-resistant spores and produce toxins
Be killed instantly at room temperature
questions.explain: Some bacteria form heat-resistant spores, and certain toxins they produce are not destroyed by normal cooking.

questions.q: What is the recommended core temperature that cooked food should reach to kill most harmful bacteria?
questions.explain: Food should be cooked to a core temperature of at least 75C to destroy most harmful bacteria.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of good personal hygiene in the kitchen?
options: Wearing the same apron for weeks
Washing hands before handling food and after touching raw meat
Tasting food with the same spoon repeatedly
questions.explain: Washing hands thoroughly before cooking and after handling raw meat helps prevent the spread of bacteria.

questions.q: A correctly working refrigerator should keep food at approximately:
questions.explain: A fridge should run at about 0-5C to slow the growth of bacteria.

questions.q: When reheating cooked food, the centre (core) should reach at least:
questions.explain: Reheated food should reach a core temperature of at least 75C to kill harmful bacteria.

questions.q: Which four conditions do most bacteria need to multiply?
questions.explain: Bacteria need warmth, moisture, food and time (plus a suitable pH) to grow and multiply.

questions.q: The '4 Cs' of food safety are cleaning, cooking, chilling and:
questions.explain: The 4 Cs are Cleaning, Cooking, Chilling and avoiding Cross-contamination.

questions.q: The temperature range known as the 'danger zone', in which bacteria multiply most rapidly, is:
questions.explain: The danger zone is 5-63C, the range in which bacteria multiply most quickly.

questions.q: Why should you avoid washing raw chicken under a running tap before cooking?
options: It can splash and spread bacteria around the kitchen
It cooks the chicken too quickly
questions.explain: Washing raw chicken splashes bacteria such as campylobacter onto surfaces, hands and other foods.

questions.q: Hot food being kept for service (hot-holding) should be held at a temperature of at least:
questions.explain: Hot food held for service must be kept at or above 63C to keep it out of the danger zone.

questions.q: Salmonella food poisoning is most commonly associated with which foods?
questions.explain: Salmonella is commonly linked to raw or undercooked poultry, eggs and other animal products.

questions.q: Bacteria in the danger zone can roughly double in number every:
questions.explain: In ideal conditions bacteria can divide approximately every 10-20 minutes, so numbers rise rapidly.
